The big picture

The giants sit on top of 400 million firms, and most of the world works informally

This page covers the whole economy around the listed giants: how many businesses exist, who employs the world, where new firms are born, and how venture capital, IPOs, M&A, sovereign funds and co-operatives move money between them.

1. The pyramid of business on Earth

Each layer is roughly 10 to 100 times smaller than the one below it. The bars use a log scale, so each gridline is 10 times the last.

For every listed company there are about 8,000 small firms

Number of firms per layer, log scale. Hover for the source of each layer.

Sources: IFC/McKinsey via CGAP (2010); IFC MSME Economic Indicators (2019); World Bank CM.MKT.LDOM.NO (2024); Forbes Global 2000 (2026); CB Insights; Fortune Global 500 (2026); Wikipedia trillion-dollar table (Oct 2026).

Only half the world's workers draw a wage

World employment by status, % of total employment (ILO modelled)

Source: ILO modelled estimates, World informality profile (2025).

Three in four Indian workers are self-employed, against about one in sixteen in the US

Self-employed as % of total employment, 1991–2025 (World Bank / ILO modelled). Choose a country to compare.

Source: World Bank SL.EMP.SELF.ZS (ILO modelled estimates). Self-employed = employers + own-account + contributing family workers.

2. Formal vs informal: most of the world's work happens outside the registers

Informal work means no contract, no social security and usually an unregistered business. Rich countries are the exception.

58% of jobs worldwide are informal, and 88% in low-income countries

Informal employment (% of total, 2024) and informal enterprises (% of all enterprises, 2019), by country income group

Source: ILO modelled estimates; ILO (2023) Women and men in the informal economy, via the ILO World informality profile.

Among large economies, India's informality is close to Nigeria's and Pakistan's

Informal employment rate, % of total employment, latest year since 2015 (harmonized ILO series). Showing the 40 largest economies with data.

Source: ILOSTAT, informal employment rate (DF_EMP_NIFL_SEX_RT), national labour force surveys. The US and China report no harmonized data.

3. Business creation: where new companies are born

New business density is the number of newly registered limited-liability companies per 1,000 people aged 15–64. It counts formal companies only, not sole proprietors.

India registers 0.18 new companies per 1,000 adults, about a hundredth of the UK's rate

New business density, latest year (2020–2024). India is highlighted.

Source: World Bank Entrepreneurship Database (IC.BUS.NDNS.ZS, IC.BUS.NREG). No US data.

India's registrations rose after 2015 but its density stays low

New business density, 2006–2024, for selected countries. Click a legend item to hide a line, or add a country.

Source: World Bank IC.BUS.NDNS.ZS. "World" is the World Bank aggregate of reporting countries.

4. Venture capital: the money behind the startups

VC hit $512B in 2025, its second-best year, and the US took two-thirds

Global VC deal value by region, US$ billion, 2019–2025 (KPMG Venture Pulse / PitchBook)

Source: KPMG Private Enterprise, Venture Pulse Q4'25 (PitchBook data, 19 Jan 2026). Annual figures are sums of the reported quarters. Rest of world is mostly Africa and Oceania.

AI went from 18% of VC dollars to 64%

Global venture funding, AI vs non-AI, US$ billion (Crunchbase)

Source: Crunchbase News year-end 2024 and 2025 analyses, Q3 2026 report. Crunchbase totals differ from KPMG's because the two use different definitions.
